en: The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha Bhagavān was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jetavana.
At the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park,
the Blessed One was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, during the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
Having traveled through that country in due order, he returned to his original location;
when the meal was finished, in the afternoon, he put away his robes and bowl and washed his feet.
As usual, he spread out his seat and sat down cross-legged, holding his body upright and establishing mindfulness before him.
Then the bhikṣus all went to where the Buddha was; having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti was seated among the great assembly.
Then the Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and knelt with his right knee on the ground.
He joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, skillfully protects and mindfully sustains all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas by means of supreme benefit."
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have been well entrusted with the unsurpassed teaching.
World-Honored One,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practices the Bodhisattva vehicle, how should they abide?
"How does one practice?
How does one give rise to the bodhicitta?
Having asked this, the Venerable Subhūti [spoke].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Subhūti:
“Subhūti, excellent, excellent!
Thus it is, noble son!
The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for the sake of supreme benefit;
he well entrusts all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for the sake of the supreme teaching.
Subhūti! Therefore, listen now with a single-minded focus, and respectfully and well contemplate this, for I shall now speak it for you.
Just as a bodhisattva who has resolved upon awakening and practices the Bodhisattva vehicle should abide, so should they practice, and so should they resolve their mind.
Subhūti replied, “So be it,
World-Honored One! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family has resolved upon bodhicitta and practices the Bodhisattva vehicle, they should resolve their mind in this way:

‘All categories of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or formless; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception; and including all that is within the realm of sentient beings and designated by conventional names—all such beings, I shall establish in *nirvāṇa* without remainder.’”
"Thus, although he has brought immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has been brought to nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva harbors the notion of a 'sentient being,' he should not be called a bodhisattva."
Why is this? Subhūti,
all bodhisattvas are without the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a recipient.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without attachment to their own kind, without attachment to others, and should practice giving without attachment to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena."
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should practice giving in this way, without clinging to the perception of signs. Why is that?
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment, this mass of merit is incalculable. Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Can the space in the eastern direction be measured? Subhūti replied:
"It is not so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, "It is even so, Subhūti!"
“Can the ten directions— the south, west, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—
the void of space, be measured? Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “So it is,
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment, this mass of merit is likewise immeasurable.”
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the excellence of his physical marks?
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
The superior marks and virtues of the body spoken of by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, superior marks and virtues."
"Why is this so, Subhūti? All that has marks is entirely false; that which is without marks is reality."
"One should perceive the Tathāgata through the non-existence of marks.
When this had been said,
the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the present time and in future ages, might there be bodhisattvas who, upon hearing the correct exposition of such signs as these—the chapters and verses of this sutra—conceive the thought that they are real?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not speak thus:

'In the present time and in future ages, will there be any bodhisattvas who, upon hearing such a correct exposition as these characteristics and the chapters and verses of this sutra, will conceive the notion that they are real?'"
Why is this? Subhūti,
in future ages there will truly be sentient beings who, upon hearing this sutra, are able to give rise to the perception of reality.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, in the future age,
during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is perishing, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who maintain the precepts, cultivate merit, and possess wisdom."
Subhūti! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not served only a single Buddha, nor have they planted roots of goodness under only a single Buddha;
they have already served immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and have already planted roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.

If there are good sons or good daughters who hear this correct exposition, such characteristics as these, and even for a single thought-moment give rise to true faith in the chapters and verses of this sutra.
Subhūti! The Tathāgata fully knows these people; the Tathāgata fully sees these people. Subhūti!
These sons and daughters of good family will produce and grow an immeasurable accumulation of merit.
Why is this? Subhūti, [it is because...]
These bodhisattvas no longer have the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a recipient.
These bodhisattvas have no notion of phenomena, nor any notion of non-phenomena; they have neither notion nor non-notion.
Why is this? Subhūti,
if these bodhisattvas have the notion of a dharma, that is precisely the grasping at a self, as well as the grasping at a sentient being, a life-span, and a recipient.
Subhūti! For this reason, a bodhisattva should not grasp at dharmas, nor should they grasp at non-dharmas.
It is for this purpose that the Tathāgata has said:
"If a practitioner of the path understands the Parable of the Raft Sūtra, even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma.
The Buddha again addressed the Venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti!"
What do you think?
Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Or has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma?

Subhūti said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has attained which is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has preached."
Why is this? This Dharma taught by the Tathāgata cannot be grasped and cannot be expressed; it is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma. Why is this?
"All noble ones are manifested through the unconditioned True Suchness. Subhūti,
what do you think?"
If one were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift, would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on account of this giving?
Subhūti said: “Very much, World-Honored One! Very much, Sugata!”
These sons and daughters of good family will, because of this giving, obtain exceedingly great merit. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
"This accumulation of merit is itself not an accumulation of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as an 'accumulation of merit. The Buddha said: "Subhūti!..."
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take the seven treasures filling the entire trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift;
and if there were another person who, from this sutra, were to receive even a single four-line verse and correctly explain and reveal its meaning to others.
The merit produced by this person through these causes and conditions is far greater than that, immeasurable and incalculable.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The unsurpassed enlightenment of the Tathāgata is accomplished through this merit; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are born from this merit.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
"What is called 'Buddha-dharma' is not Buddha-dharma; it is merely designated as 'Buddha-dharma.
Subhūti, what do you think?
Can a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) form this thought:
"I have attained the fruit of stream-entry"? No.
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One! Why is this so?
"Bhagavān! In reality, there is nothing whatsoever that can reach the stream; therefore, one is called a *srotāpanna*.
This applies likewise to form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*); for this reason, one is named a *srotāpanna*."
The Sakṛdāgāmin is called "one who comes back once"; yet in reality there is nothing that can come back, and thus he is named a Sakṛdāgāmin.
The Anāgāmin is called "one who does not come back"; yet in reality there is nothing that can not come back, and thus he is named an Anāgāmin.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
Can an Arhat form this thought:
"I have attained the fruit of Arhatship"? No.
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One! Why is this so?”
"In truth, there is nothing whatsoever that is called an 'Arhat,' World-Honored One!
If an Arhat were to have such a thought:"
“‘I have attained the fruit of arhatship’—
this, World-Honored One, is precisely the grasping at a self, the grasping at a sentient being, the grasping at a life-span, and the grasping at a recipient.”
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has praised me, saying that among those who dwell in the samādhi of non-contention, I am the foremost.
World-Honored One!
I have now become an Arhat, free from the desires of the three realms of existence.
World-Honored One!
I also do not harbor such a thought as: ‘I am an arhat.’
"World-Honored One!
If I were to have this thought:
'I have already attained the fruit of Arhatship.'"
If that were so, the Tathāgata would not have bestowed upon me this prediction:
"Among those who dwell in the samādhi of non-contention, the son of good family Subhūti is the foremost."
"In truth, there is no abiding; one abides in non-contention, one abides in non-contention.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
“Formerly, from the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, was there even a single dharma that the Tathāgata took up?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"In truth, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has ever received from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If there should be a bodhisattva who speaks thus:"
"I shall adorn a pure buddha-field"—
this bodhisattva speaks a false word. Why is this?
Subhūti! That which is called the adornment of Buddha-fields, the Tathāgata says is not an adornment; it is therefore called the adornment of pure Buddha-fields. Subhūti!

Therefore, a bodhisattva should give rise to such a mind that is free from dwelling and attachment; they should not give rise to a mind that dwells in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas, but should give rise to that mind by dwelling in nothing at all.
“Subhūti! For example, suppose there were a person whose physical form was as vast and great as Sumeru, the king of mountains. Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Is such a body and its characteristics supreme and great? Subhūti replied:
“Very great, World-Honored One! Why is this?
That which the Tathāgata calls ‘having a body’ is, in truth, not having a body.”
"This is not existent; therefore, it is called 'having a body.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
“Regarding all the grains of sand in the Ganges River, if there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand therein, would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be numerous?
Subhūti replied, “They would be very numerous, World-Honored One!”
"Yet even all those Ganges Rivers are already incalculably many; how much more so their sands? The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
I now awaken you; I now show you this:

if there were as many worlds as there are grains of sand in all the Ganges Rivers, and if some son or daughter of good family were to fill them entirely with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Subhūti, what do you think? Would this person,
by reason of these causes and conditions, acquire much merit?
Subhūti said: “Very much, World-Honored One! Very much, Sugata!”
"By this cause and condition, this person generates exceedingly great merit. Subhūti!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take the seven treasures and fill as many worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers, and offer them as a gift."
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from this sutra down to even a single four-line verse, respectfully receives and upholds it and correctly expounds it for others,
the merit produced by this person will be far more supreme than that, immeasurable and incalculable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

In whatever place there may be someone who can read, recite, or explain from this sutra even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that such a place becomes a caitya within the world."
All humans, devas, asuras, and others should pay them respect;

how much more so those who are able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite such a sutra as this! You should know that such persons are in harmony with the unsurpassed and rare Dharma, and that in whatever land or place they dwell, the Great Teacher is present therein, or at least some person worthy of veneration is found.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words,
the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What is the name of this sutra, and how shall we uphold it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This sutra is named 'The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā'; by this name you should uphold it.
Why is that? Subhūti!"
This prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata has said, is not prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti,
what do you think?
“Is there even a single dharma that has been taught by a Buddha?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"There is not a single dharma that a Tathāgata has taught.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many?"
Subhūti said: "These atoms of this world, Blessed One, are exceedingly many;
exceedingly many, Sugata!"
Why is this? World-Honored One!
These atoms, as the Tathāgata has said, are not atoms; therefore they are called atoms.
"These worlds, the Tathāgata has said, are not worlds; therefore they are called 'worlds.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think?"
“Can one see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? These thirty-two marks of a great man, the Tathāgata has said, are not marks; therefore they are called the thirty-two marks of a great man.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there were good sons or good daughters who, for as many times as there are grains of sand in all the Ganges Rivers, were to give up their own lives and bodies in such numbers as those grains of sand to practice giving; [and if another were to hear this Dharma and gain faith, the latter would generate a far greater merit than the former]."
If there are good sons or good daughters who, from this sutra down to even a single four-line verse, reverently accept and uphold it and correctly expound it for others.
"By this cause and condition, this person will generate merit far greater than that, immeasurable and incalculable.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, moved by the swift power of the Dharma, immediately wept; wiping away his tears, he said:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
How rare, Sugata! Regarding this sūtra spoken by the Tathāgata, from the time I first attained noble wisdom until now, I have never before heard such a sūtra being taught.
Why is this? World-Honored One, when you speak of the perfection of wisdom, it is not [in fact] the perfection of wisdom; therefore it is called the "perfection of wisdom.
World-Honored One!
It should be known that such a person is endowed with the unsurpassed and most rare Dharma, for when hearing the sutra being preached, they are able to give rise to the perception of reality.
World-Honored One!
This "perception of reality" is, in truth, not a perception; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "perception of reality," and speaks of it as the "perception of reality."
"Bhagavān! For me, this is not a rare occurrence; as you were correctly teaching the sūtra, I gave rise to faith and understanding. Bhagavān!"

If there are sentient beings in future ages who respectfully receive and uphold this [teaching] and correctly expound it for others, you should know that such persons will be endowed with the unsurpassed and most rare Dharma.
World-Honored One!
This person no longer has the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a recipient. Why is this?
The notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, and the notion of a recipient are, in fact, not notions. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have liberated themselves from all notions, leaving none remaining.
Having spoken these words,
the Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is, Subhūti!”
It is so. You should know that such a person is endowed with the unsurpassed and most rare Dharma;
upon hearing this sutra being preached, they are not startled, not terrified, and do not fear it.
Why is this? Subhūti! This Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is the foremost pāramitā.
This perfection has been taught by the Tathāgata, and immeasurable Buddhas have likewise taught it; therefore, it is called the foremost perfection.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, this perfection of patience of the Tathāgata is not a perfection."
Why is this? Subhūti, in the past,
when I was King Kaliṅga, my body was hacked and cut until my flesh and bones were shattered and scattered.
At that time, I had no notion of a self, no notion of a sentient being, no notion of a life-span, and no notion of a recipient; I had neither a notion nor a non-notion. Why was this?

Subhūti! If, at that time, I had possessed the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a recipient, then at that moment I would have given rise to thoughts of resentment.
Subhūti! I recall that during five hundred past lives, I was a great rishi named Kṣāntivādin.
During those lifetimes, my mind was free from the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, and the notion of a recipient.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should relinquish all perceptions and should resolve upon unsurpassed awakening; they should not give rise to a mind that dwells on form, nor should they give rise to a mind that dwells on sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles; they should not give rise to a mind that dwells on mental phenomena (*dharma*), nor should they give rise to a mind that dwells on non-phenomena (*adharma*), nor should they give rise to a mind that dwells anywhere at all.
Why is this? If the mind has a dwelling place, it is not truly dwelling.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says:
“A bodhisattva should practice giving with a mind that dwells nowhere. Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva should practice giving in this way for the benefit of all sentient beings.
This notion of "sentient beings" is itself non-notion.
Thus, all these sentient beings spoken of by the Tathāgata are themselves non-sentient beings. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are far removed from all conceptualizations. "Subhūti!
That which the Tathāgata speaks is reality, he speaks truth, he speaks suchness, and he speaks that which is not false."
Furthermore, Subhūti!
This Dharma is that which the Tathāgata has awakened to; this Dharma is that which the Tathāgata has preached; this Dharma is neither real nor unreal. Subhūti!
Subhūti, it is as if there were a person in total darkness; in this same way, you should know that a bodhisattva who falls into the practice of signs and falls into giving with signs is like that.
Subhūti, it is as if a person with eyes, when the night has turned to dawn and the light of the sun shines during the day, sees various forms.
In this way, you should know that the bodhisattva does not fall into signs when practicing signless giving.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, in future ages, if there are good men or good women who receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice such a sutra as this, and correctly explain it to others, the Tathāgata fully knows these people and fully sees these people; they shall grow a boundless accumulation of merit."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If there were good sons or good daughters who, during the morning portion of the day, gave away their bodies and lives as many times as there are grains of sand in the rivers mentioned above."

During the midday period, he distributed his body and life as alms; during the afternoon period, he likewise distributed his body and life as alms, each time in numbers equal to the sands of all the rivers as previously described.
In this manner, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, he gave away his body and life as alms.
If there should be another person who, upon hearing this sutra, does not give rise to slander,
by this cause and condition they will produce merit far more numerous and immeasurable than that;
how much more so for one who copies it, receives and maintains it, reads and recites it, teaches others to practice it, and explains it extensively for others?
"Furthermore, Subhūti, such a sūtra as this is inconceivable and peerless;
the Tathāgata teaches it only out of compassion and for the benefit of those who can practice the Unsurpassed Vehicle and the Peerless Vehicle."

Furthermore, if there should be anyone in future ages who receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, and teaches others to practice it and correctly expound it, the Tathāgata fully knows these people and fully sees these people; they shall be endowed with an immeasurable, infinite, inconceivable, and peerless mass of merit.
Such persons as these, by means of my own body, will be able to bear the burden of unsurpassed bodhi.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Regarding such a sutra as this, it is impossible for those who have inferior aspirations and desires, or those who hold views of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, or a recipient—such persons as these—to be able to hear, practice, read, recite, or correctly teach it to others.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Wherever this sutra is expounded, all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and so forth—should make offerings, pay homage, and circumambulate it to the right."
"You should know that this place in the world becomes a caitya.
Subhūti! If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, recite, teach others to practice, and correctly expound such sūtras as these."

If this person currently undergoes such things as being treated with contempt and disdain, the evil karma they created in past lives—which would otherwise have resulted in rebirth in the evil realms—is instead exhausted by the experience of slight suffering in the present life. Consequently, their past sins and the resulting bitter retribution are extinguished, and they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Subhūti! I recall that in the past, beyond countless, immeasurable eons past calculation, after the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, eighty-four hundred thousand koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas attained parinirvāṇa; I served, made offerings to, and honored them all, never letting my service go to waste.”

Furthermore, Subhūti, if there should be someone in the final age, during the final five hundred years, who receives, maintains, reads, recites, teaches others to practice, and correctly explains this sutra. Subhūti!

The mass of merit produced by this person cannot be matched by even a hundredth part of the merit I obtained from serving and making offerings to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the past; it does not reach even a ten-thousand-millionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation, nor even by any analogy corresponding to its power or category.

“Subhūti! If I were to fully describe the merit obtained by good sons and good daughters who, in the final age at the end of time, receive, uphold, read, and recite such sūtras as these, then if any good son or good daughter were to listen attentively and remember that mass of merit, their minds might become confused or even go mad.”
Furthermore, Subhūti, such a sūtra as this is inconceivable;
the practice of it by persons and the attainment of its fruit are likewise inconceivable.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a son of good family or a daughter of good family, who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practices the Bodhisattva vehicle, abide?”
"How does one practice?
How does one generate the bodhicitta?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Good sons and good daughters who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should give rise to this thought:
‘I shall establish all sentient beings and cause them to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.’”
"Thus, although he has brought immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has been brought to nirvāṇa.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
If a bodhisattva has the notion of a sentient being, then they should not be called a "bodhisattva.
Why is that? Subhūti!
In reality, there is no dharma that can be called "one who practices the Bodhisattva's Supreme Vehicle.
Subhūti, what do you think?
"At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, was there even a single dharma that the Tathāgata obtained which is called 'anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One."
"At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was not a single dharma that the Tathāgata obtained which could be called 'anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi'.
The Buddha said, "So it is, Subhūti!"
It is so. Under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was not a single dharma that the Tathāgata obtained which could be called "anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti!

If, at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there were even a single dharma that the Tathāgata had obtained which could be called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed upon me this prediction: "O Brahmin!..."
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Subhūti!

Because there is, in reality, no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for this reason the Buddha Dīpaṃkara conferred upon me the prediction, speaking these words: "O Brahmin!..."
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
For what reason?
Subhūti! "Tathāgata" is another name for True Suchness (tathatā). Subhūti!
If anyone says, "The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," that person speaks untruthfully.
Why is this? Subhūti,
there is truly no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained which is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! This Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is neither real nor unreal; therefore, the Tathāgata says:
"All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas."
“Subhūti! All dharmas are not all dharmas; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of them by the name ‘all dharmas. Subhūti!”
“It is, for example, like a person with a body that is vast throughout its entirety. Subhūti said,
“World-Honored One!”
"This 'omnipresent great body' spoken of by the Tathāgata is, in fact, no body; therefore it is called the 'omnipresent great body.
The Buddha said, "So it is, Subhūti!"
"So it is, Subhūti! If there is a bodhisattva who speaks these words:"
"Subhūti, if one were to think, 'I shall bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa,' then one should not be called a bodhisattva."
"What do you think?
Is there even a single dharma that can be called 'bodhisattva'? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said: "Subhūti!
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said:
"All dharmas are without self, without a sentient being, without a life-span, and without a recipient. Subhūti!
If there is a bodhisattva who speaks these words:
"I shall adorn and purify a buddha-field," such a bodhisattva speaks false and deceptive words.
Why is this? Subhūti!
That which is called the adornment of Buddha-fields, the Tathāgata says is not an adornment; it is therefore called the adornment of pure Buddha-fields.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, through faith, perceives that all phenomena are without self and that all phenomena are without self, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha says:
"This is called a bodhisattva; this is called a bodhisattva."
"Subhūti! What do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye?"
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.”
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? Subhūti replied,
“It is so, World-Honored One!”
"The Tathāgata possesses the divine eye. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?”
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye.”
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, what do you think?”
“Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
Subhūti replied, “It is so, World-Honored One!”
“The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. “Subhūti,
what do you think?”

"As many grains of sand as there are in the river Ganges, that many Ganges rivers there might be; and as many worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges rivers—would these not be very many?"
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One!
The number of these worlds is exceedingly great.”
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! As for all the sentient beings in those worlds, I see and know them all, abiding in their mental continuums with various kinds of dispositions.”
Why is this? Subhūti, the continuous dwelling of the mind, the Tathāgata says, is not a continuous dwelling; therefore it is called "continuous dwelling."
Why is this? Subhūti!
The past mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended.
“Subhūti, what do you think?
If someone were to give away as a gift the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm, would that son or daughter of good family obtain much merit on account of this cause and condition?”
Subhūti said: "Very much, World-Honored One! Very much, Sugata!"
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti! So it is.”
"By this causal condition, that son or daughter of good family will have a vast accumulation of merit. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
If the mass of merit were merely a "mass," then the Tathāgata would not have said, "This is a mass of merit; this is a mass of merit.
Subhūti, what do you think?
“Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of the physical body?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
One should not view the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of the physical body.

Why is this? This so-called "perfection of the physical body" has been taught by the Tathāgata as not being a perfection of the physical body; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "perfection of the physical body."
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the possession of the various marks?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of the primary marks. Why is this?
These so-called "perfections of marks" were taught by the Tathāgata as being non-perfections; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of them as the perfection of marks.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
Does the Tathāgata have such an intention as this:
"I am now truly teaching the Dharma"?
Subhūti! If someone were to say:
"The Tathāgata truly can preach the Dharma," [they would speak falsely].
"You should know, Subhūti, that this person, by means of what is not truly existent and through false attachment, gives rise to slander against me.
Why is this? Subhūti!"
"To speak of the Dharma, to speak of the Dharma—truly there is no dharma that can be called 'speaking of the Dharma.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing such passages of this sutra as these correctly explained, will give rise to true faith?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"They are not sentient beings, nor are they non-sentient beings."
Why is this? Subhūti!
Those beings whom the Tathāgata calls "beings" are not beings, nor are they non-beings; therefore, he speaks of them as "beings."
Subhūti, what do you think?
Is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has attained which is called "anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi"?
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One!
There is not a single dharma that the Tathāgata has attained which is called ‘anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti! So it is.”

There is not even a dharma as small as a mote of dust that the Tathāgata has relinquished or that the Tathāgata has attained; therefore, it is called the absolute equality of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! The awakening of all Buddhas is without distinction; therefore, it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! This Dharma is equal, without high or low; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore, Subhūti..."
Because it is without self, without sentient beings, without life-span, and without a recipient, this Dharma is equal; therefore, it is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! By means of genuine wholesome dharmas, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in full perfection. Subhūti!"
Regarding what is called "wholesome dharmas," Subhūti, the Tathāgata says they are not dharmas; therefore they are called "wholesome dharmas. "Subhūti!..."
If there were as many heaps of the seven treasures as all the Sumeru Kings of Mountains throughout the trichiliocosm, and someone were to take these and give them as a gift;

If a person, from this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* down to even a single four-line verse, should receive, uphold, read, recite, and correctly explain it to others, the merit they obtain compared to the former merit does not equal even one hundredth part; it does not equal one ten-million-billionth part; it cannot be reached by any calculation, nor can it be approached by any power, category, or corresponding analogy.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata have this thought:”
"Subhūti, do you think that one thinks, 'I deliver sentient beings'?"
You should not now entertain such a thought.
Why is this? In reality, there are no sentient beings who are delivered by the Tathāgata.

Subhūti! If there were any sentient beings who were liberated by the Tathāgata, that would constitute grasping at a self, grasping at a sentient being, grasping at a life-span, and grasping at a recipient.
Subhūti! This grasping at a self, the Tathāgata has said is not grasping, for it is the grasping of infantile, ordinary worldlings. Subhūti!
“Those who are infantile ordinary beings, the Tathāgata says they are not beings; therefore, he speaks of ‘infantile ordinary beings.
Subhūti, what do you think?”
"Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the marks of physical perfection? Subhūti replied,
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the marks of physical perfection."
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti! So it is.”
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the possession of marks. Why is this?

If one were to perceive the Tathāgata by means of the possession of marks, then a Wheel-turning Sage King (cakravartin) would also be the Tathāgata; therefore, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the possession of marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one sees me by means of form, Or seeks me by means of sound,
Such a person follows a deviant path And shall not be able to see me."
One should see the Buddha through the Dharma; the Tamer has the Dharma as his body.
This Dharma is not the sphere of consciousness; the suchness of the Dharma is profound and difficult to perceive. "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Can a Tathāgata attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection?
Subhūti, [the Buddha said: "Subhūti!"
You should not now hold such a view as this:
"The Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection. Why is that?
Subhūti! The Tathāgata does not attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of being endowed with the marks. Subhūti!
If you should think: "The Tathāgata has said that for one who practices the vehicle of the bodhisattva, there is a dharma that can be extinguished," Subhūti!
Do not hold such a view. Why is this?
The Tathāgata does not say that for those who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle there is any dharma that can be extinguished or eternally severed.
“Subhūti! If there were good sons or good daughters who, taking the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, used them to practice giving as an act of charity;”
If there is a bodhisattva who, regarding all phenomena as selfless and unarisen, attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas,
by this cause and condition, the merit they obtain is far greater than that [of the former].
“Subhūti! One who practices the Mahāyāna should not grasp at the accumulation of merit. Subhūti said:
“Can this mass of merit be grasped? The Buddha said, “Subhūti!...”
This mass of merit can be gathered and maintained, but it cannot be grasped; therefore, it is said that this mass of merit should be gathered and maintained. Subhūti!
If someone were to say,
"The Tathāgata walks, stands, sits, or lies down," that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? Subhūti, the Tathāgata has nowhere to go and nowhere from which he comes; for this reason, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

“Subhūti! Suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take the earth-element atoms of a trichiliocosm, burn them to ashes, and form them into ink pellets as numerous as a heap of those very atoms.”
Subhūti, what do you think? Is this collection of atoms indeed much?
Subhūti said: "That mass of atoms is very great,
World-Honored One!"
Why is this? World-Honored One!
If the aggregation of atoms were substantially existent, then the World-Honored One would not refer to it by the name "aggregation of atoms."

Why is this? That which the World-Honored One has spoken of as an aggregation of atoms, the Tathāgata has said is not an aggregation of atoms; it is for this reason that it is called an "aggregation of atoms."
That which the Tathāgata has spoken of as the trichiliocosm is not a world; therefore it is called the "trichiliocosm. Why is this so?
World-Honored One!

If one clings to the world as being substantially existent, that is the clinging to a collection as a unity. This clinging to a collection as a unity, the Tathāgata says, is not clinging; therefore he speaks of "clinging to a collection as a unity."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
“Subhūti! This 'grasping at a collection' is merely a worldly convention.”
Subhūti! This Dharma is not a dharma that can be expressed in words; it is grasped through the biased speech of infantile, ordinary worldlings. Subhūti!
Subhūti, if someone were to say:
"The Tathāgata has spoken of the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of a recipient," [they would speak falsely].
"What do you think?
Is the speech of such a person considered right speech? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata! Why is this so?

The views of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, and a recipient spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not views; it is for this reason that they are called the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of a recipient.
“Subhūti! If a person practices the Bodhisattva vehicle, they should know, see, and believe in this way; they should cultivate all dharmas in this way so that the notion of ‘dharmas’ does not arise.”
Why is this? Subhūti!
This so-called "conception of dharmas," the Tathāgata has said that it is not a conception; therefore, he speaks of the "conception of dharmas."
“Subhūti! If there were a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with the seven treasures filling countless and immeasurable worlds, were to offer them as a gift;

and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, from this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra down to even a single four-line verse, were to receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and teach others to practice it and explain it extensively for them—[the latter would generate far more merit].”
By these causes and conditions, the merit produced by these good sons and good daughters will be far greater than that, immeasurable and incalculable.
How then shall this sutra be clearly expounded?
Because there is nothing to be manifested in what is taught, it is called "manifest teaching.
Just as suchness is immovable, there is always the correct teaching.
One should contemplate conditioned phenomena as being like darkness, cataracts, a lamp, a phantom, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud.

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti’s heart was filled with joy and inspiration; likewise, the assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as all the world—including humans, devas, and asuras—leaped for joy and, with faith and acceptance, put it into practice.
The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra
